title: 5 Reasons You Should Never, Ever Narrate
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin defines narration as any talking a teacher does while students are supposed to be independently carrying out a task the teacher already assigned, including reminding, repeating directions, praising, or describing what students are doing. He argues that narration is uniformly harmful, even when it feels supportive, because it removes the incentive for students to listen the first time and trains them to wait for verbal hand-holding. He walks through five specific costs: weakened listening, learned helplessness, boredom, immaturity, and wasted time, each building on the idea that constant teacher talk strips students of ownership over their own performance. The corrective he proposes is to teach and model with clarity, check for understanding, give a clear 'go' signal, and then stay completely silent while students work, sending anyone who fails back through reteaching rather than narrating them through it. He frames silence after instructions as an act of trust that forces students to develop independence, maturity, and genuine engagement.
points: Narration is any teacher talk during a task students were already told to do on their own, including reminders, praise, and restated directions.
Narrating weakens listening because students learn they don't need to catch directions the first time.
Constant verbal guidance produces learned helplessness by removing students' need to problem-solve.
The fix is silence after the 'go' signal, with failure sent back to reteaching rather than narrated through.
Ending narration produces a more capable, independent class across all five problem areas at once.
quotes: narration is any talking by the teacher while students are meant to be performing a task that was asked of them.
When students realize you’re going to talk them through directions that you’ve just given them, then you remove any reason for them to listen to you the first time.
Narration lightens responsibility. It subverts and subdues problem-solving skills. It causes students to shut off their brain and rely on you to do their thinking for them.
If you treat your students like helpless babies, then that’s how they’ll behave. The key to maturity is to push the limits on your expectations and load up on responsibility.
Never, ever remind or repeat yourself while your students are in the process. Never say a word. Just observe and verify that it’s done as taught.
It’s all you, you, you—talking, guiding, reminding, and praising them through every little this and that, which, sadly, they can do perfectly well if only given the chance.
